diagnostic_evidence.quote: when $\omega > 1$ is used (which is the case of interest in overrelaxation) it cannot be guaranteed that positive definite matrices are generated
\bS_\omega\!\begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \end{pmatrix} =  \begin{pmatrix} (1-\omega) X + \omega S_1(Y) \\ (1-\omega) Y + \omega S_2((1-\omega) X + \omega S_1(Y)) \end{pmatrix}

issues.failure_explanation: The text asserts that, for a neighborhood O of Y_* only, S_omega maps C_m x O into C_m x C_n. For omega > 1 the first component (1-omega)X + omega S_1(Y) is not positive definite when X is large relative to S_1(Y) (e.g. Y = Y_*, X = 100 X_*, omega = 1.5 gives -48.5 X_* which is negative definite), so the second component's inverse need not exist and the map is not into C_m x C_n. Well-definedness holds only on a neighborhood of (X_*,Y_*) in both variables (and by equivariance on a neighborhood of the orbit), which is what is actually used later.

failure_location.quote: is well defined as a map from $\caC_m \times \mathcal O$ to $\caC_m \times \caC_n$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the domain statement by: S_omega is well defined on a neighborhood of (X_*,Y_*) in C_m x C_n (depending on omega), and hence, by equivariance, on a neighborhood of the orbit.
issues.overall_effect: Only the stated domain of S_omega in Section 3.1 is wrong; Lemma lem: equal derivatives and Theorem thm: local convergence only use well-definedness in a neighborhood of the fixed point/orbit, which remains valid.
issues.title: Euclidean SOR map S_omega claimed well defined on all of C_m x O, which fails for omega > 1
issues.why_classification: A local correction of a domain statement; no result, rate, or method depends on the incorrect wider domain.

issues.failure_explanation: Taking traces of sum_i x~_i x~_i^T = I_n forces sum_i ||x~_i||^2 = n, i.e. ||x~_i||_2^2 = n/k, not ||x~_i||_2 = n/k; with n = 50, k = 55 the stated frame scaling problem has no solution. Moreover, from the operator scaling conditions ell_i^2 ||R x_i||^2 = 1/k and sum ell_i^2 R x_i x_i^T R^T = I_n/n, the correct correspondence is x~_i = sqrt(n) ell_i R x_i, i.e. alpha_i = sqrt(n) ell_i; the stated alpha_i = n ell_i^2 gives sum x~_i x~_i^T = n^2 sum ell_i^4 R x_i x_i^T R^T, which is not I_n in general. Thus the claimed equivalence is false as written.

failure_location.quote: So $P = R$ and $\alpha_i = n\ell_i^2$ yield a solution to frame scaling, and vice versa.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the norm constraint by ||x~_i||_2^2 = n/k (equivalently ||x~_i||_2 = sqrt(n/k)) and the correspondence by alpha_i = sqrt(n) ell_i (with ell_i > 0).
issues.overall_effect: The reduction of frame scaling to operator scaling used to motivate the first experiment is misstated; the experiment itself (operator scaling with A_i = e_i x_i^T) and all theoretical results are unaffected.
issues.title: Frame scaling formulation and the stated correspondence to operator scaling are inconsistent
issues.why_classification: Two local formula corrections restore a correct equivalence; nothing else in the paper depends on the erroneous formulas.
